_README: THE POPULATION REFERENCE. Every number here was read off a named public source on a
named date, and nothing here is interpolated, rounded to taste or filled in. That rule
is the whole point: tools/probe-crowd.mjs refused to score the profiles for months
because a WRONG reference is worse than none — the same rule that keeps invented values
out of the profiles themselves. If a number is not in a source below, it is absent here
and the tool prints a dash rather than guessing.
BOTH SOURCES ARE BIASED, and the bias is written into each entry rather than mentioned
once and forgotten. Read `bias` before using a number to argue anything.
THE UNITS TRAP, which is why the two sources disagree and both are right. Steam reports
the PHYSICAL display resolution the OS is set to. A browser reports screen.width in CSS
pixels — physical divided by devicePixelRatio — which is why StatCounter's table is full
of resolutions no panel is manufactured in: 1536x864 is a 1920x1080 panel at 125% Windows
scaling, and 1280x720 is the same panel at 150%. Measured on this project's own rig with
--force-device-scale-factor: screen.availWidth is exactly physical/dpr. So a profile's
CLAIMED PANEL is screenW * dpr, and that is a different question from what screen.width
should be. Both are scored below, against the source that actually measures each.

screen_css_px.source: StatCounter Global Stats — Desktop Screen Resolution, Worldwide
screen_css_px.measures: screen.width x screen.height as the BROWSER reports it, i.e. CSS pixels
bias: Page-view weighted, not user weighted: heavy browsers count more than light ones.
'Desktop' is StatCounter's own classification and leaks — the 384x832 row below is
plainly not a desktop panel, and it sits at 4.33%, so treat the whole table as having
a few points of misfiled traffic in it.
Worldwide. A per-country table exists and would matter, because the profile is paired
with a country; it is not recorded here.
screen_css_px.completeness: TOP SIX ONLY. The site renders the tail with JavaScript and it was not readable; the remaining ~51% is not recorded. A resolution absent from this list is NOT thereby rare — it is unmeasured.
screen_css_px._exclude_why: 384x832 is StatCounter mis-filing mobile traffic into its desktop bucket. It is not a gap in the profile set; a desktop profile claiming it would be the defect.

notes.384x832: not a desktop panel; StatCounter's device classification leaking

ram_gb.source: Steam Hardware & Software Survey — System RAM
ram_gb.maps_to: navigator.deviceMemory, which Chrome reports as the RAM rounded DOWN to a power of two. Measured on the host of this repo: 16. There is no cap at 8 in this browser — that was checked rather than assumed.
bias: GAMERS. This is the strongest bias in the file and it points one way: Steam's
population has far more RAM than the web's. 32 GB at 36.93% is not a fact about
browsers, it is a fact about people who install Steam.
So: a value that is common HERE may be uncommon on the web, but a value that is
uncommon here is almost certainly uncommon on the web too. Use it as an upper bound
on how well-equipped a machine can be while still being ordinary.

cpu_physical_cores.source: Steam Hardware & Software Survey — Physical CPUs
cpu_physical_cores.maps_to: NOTHING DIRECTLY, and this entry exists to say so. navigator.hardwareConcurrency reports LOGICAL processors — 6 physical cores with SMT is 12, and Intel's hybrid parts break even that rule. The host of this repo reports 18. No public source measuring the logical count was found, so the profiles' 4/8/12/16 are NOT scored against this table; it is here as context and as a marker that the right table is missing.
bias: GAMERS, as above.

gpu_model.source: Steam Hardware & Software Survey — Video Card Description
bias: GAMERS, and here the bias is disqualifying rather than merely strong. Steam's list is
dominated by discrete NVIDIA parts because its population buys them; the web at large
runs mostly on Intel integrated graphics. So this table says which DISCRETE card is
commonest among gamers, and says nothing usable about how common a GPU string is on
the web.
Consequence for this project: the two Intel rows cannot be scored from here AT ALL,
and the two NVIDIA rows can only be compared to each other. No source measuring GPU
share across general web traffic was found.
gpu_model.completeness: top four rows as published; every one of them is discrete NVIDIA, which is itself the evidence for the bias above

physical_panel.source: Steam Hardware & Software Survey — Primary Display Resolution
physical_panel.measures: PHYSICAL primary display resolution, i.e. screenW * dpr for a browser
bias: GAMERS — over-represents large and high-refresh panels, and under-represents the
1366x768 office laptop almost to nothing.

notes.7680x4320: NOT in the table at any position. 8K panels exist as products but do not appear in a four-row top list where the fourth row is already at 4.95%.
notes.2880x1620: NOT in the table either, but it is a REAL manufactured panel — Lenovo ThinkPad W540/W550/T540p, ASUS Vivobook Pro 15 OLED '2.8K'. Rare, not invented.
